claim.date_text_original: Habeas corpus proceeding in Sitka, April-May 1886; decision 8 May 1886
claim.spatial_precision: Sitka local/court context; no Tlingit-wide or Alaska-wide practice inference
claim.summary: The 1886 Sah Quah habeas corpus proceeding at Sitka documented a man whom the respondent claimed to hold as a slave and chattel. The published decision records Sah Quah's testimony that he had been captured and sold as a boy and that others appropriated his labor, and it ordered his release. The atlas records a bounded local slavery-status/practice claim for the Sitka case without adopting the court's sweeping descriptions as a prevalence claim for Tlingit society.
claim.notes: The Federal Reporter decision is direct legal evidence for the case and release order, but Sidney Harring's specialist legal history shows the litigation was a deliberately framed assimilationist test case and that Sah Quah's testimony complicated the asserted owner-slave relationship. Preserve that qualification; do not generalize one case into regional prevalence or universal Tlingit practice.

territorial_practice.notes: Bounded case-level classification only. No P-level, population share, continuous interval, Tlingit-wide inference, Alaska-wide inference, or regional practice polygon.

source.title: In re Sah Quah, 31 F. 327
source.author_or_institution: United States District Court, District of Alaska; Federal Reporter
source.independence_notes: Published legal record of the habeas corpus case. Allegations, respondent return, testimony and judicial findings are different parts of one case record and must not be counted as independent attestations.
source.reliability_limitations: The judge's broad characterizations of Alaska Native/Tlingit society reflect nineteenth-century legal and assimilationist assumptions. Use the record for the bounded case, not as an uncritical ethnographic prevalence source.

version.version_label: Federal Reporter vol. 31, pp. 327-331; digitized reporter text

evidence.notes: Do not treat the court's general ethnographic assertions as a second evidence family.

source.title: The Incorporation of Alaskan Natives Under American Law: United States and Tlingit Sovereignty, 1867-1900
source.geographic_scope: Alaska, with detailed Sitka/Tlingit legal history
source.independence_notes: Specialist legal-historical interpretation of the case and archival transcript. It is not an independent occurrence witness to Sah Quah's alleged status.
source.reliability_limitations: Used to qualify the adversarial quality and assimilationist framing of the reported case, not to negate the existence of the proceeding or create a different prevalence estimate.
